questions.q: What should open the conversation with the Operations Manager?
options: The answer itself — which category sold the most units and which earned the most revenue — stated in one or two sentences
A detailed walkthrough of how the Glue Crawler and Athena query were built
A list of everything that was explicitly out of scope for this project
The full raw SQL query, so the stakeholder can verify it themselves
questions.explain: The stakeholder asked a business question and wants the answer first; the pipeline details aren't what they came for.

questions.q: Why does this result need to present two different "winners" instead of one?
options: Camp Kitchen sold the most units while Tents & Shelters earned the most revenue, and both facts are relevant to a restocking decision
Athena requires every query result to report at least two leading rows
The Operations Manager asked for exactly two separate reports
There is no real leader in either metric, so two are shown for balance
questions.explain: The two metrics genuinely point to different categories, and surfacing both prevents a restocking decision based on only half the picture.

questions.q: Why does bolding both leading values in the summary table help, rather than just listing the numbers?
options: It makes the nuance (two different leaders on two different metrics) visible at a glance instead of requiring the reader to compare every row mentally
Bold formatting is required by Athena's query result format
It hides the lower-performing categories from the stakeholder
It converts the table into a chart automatically
questions.explain: Visual emphasis on both leaders communicates the key nuance faster than requiring the reader to scan and compare rows themselves.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say it matters to mention that returns and cancellations aren't backed out of this result?
options: A few canceled high-ticket orders could shift a category's revenue more than the same cancellations would shift a cheaper category's, so leaving it unmentioned risks a misleading impression of confidence
Athena cannot technically process returns data under any circumstances
Returns data does not exist anywhere in Northfield's systems
Mentioning caveats is only required when the stakeholder explicitly asks for them
questions.explain: Naming real limitations briefly is what makes a result trustworthy rather than a confident-sounding guess — especially since returns could disproportionately affect high-ticket categories.

questions.q: Why is this result called a "snapshot" rather than a dashboard?
options: It's a one-time result for a single month, not something that updates automatically on a schedule
It only shows one row of data instead of multiple categories
Snapshots are a specific AWS service distinct from Athena
It was generated without using SQL at all
questions.explain: This is a one-off answer to one question; a recurring, auto-updating version of this is explicitly called out as a bigger, different (Intermediate-tier) project.
